entries.text: Choose stronger multi-factor authentication (MFA) , including authenticator apps and phishing-resistant security keys. Protect your home Wi-Fi, router, and BYOD devices. Verify unexpected requests through a separate, trusted channel. Practice updating, password management, and prompt incident reporting. entries.text:
Watch time: 6 min 58 sec 
 Watch the video, then review the main practices below before moving on. Quick Summary 
 Remote work introduces cybersecurity risks that require extra
 precautions to protect sensitive information. Using strong
 authentication and multi-factor authentication (MFA), connecting
 through a VPN when required, and keeping software updated help
 strengthen security. Remote workers should also secure their home
 networks, use company-approved devices, stay alert to phishing
 attacks, and share files only through trusted platforms. Maintaining ongoing cybersecurity awareness helps reduce threats
 and creates a safer remote working environment.

entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: Protect your accounts with stronger MFA
entries.text: Remote work relies on accounts accessible from many locations. Passwords alone are not enough, but not all MFA methods provide the same protection.

entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: {{ item.title }}
Safe Practices for Remote Work: Important Wi-Fi distinction
entries.text: For most home routers, use WPA3-Personal or WPA2-AES if WPA3 is unavailable. WPA2-Enterprise is generally for managed business networks, not ordinary home routers. Put untrusted smart-home devices on a separate guest or IoT network where isolation is supported; keep work devices on the trusted network. Key takeaway Change default router administrator credentials, install updates, use strong Wi-Fi encryption, and separate less-trusted devices.

entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: Verify unexpected requests independently
entries.text: Any surprise request involving money, passwords, account access, or sensitive files deserves a second check using contact information you already trust. Example: A client emails revised payment details for your next invoice. The message looks familiar, but the bank account is new. Call the client using the number in your existing contract or saved directory — not the number supplied in that message.

entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: ✕ Trust the message
entries.text: Reply to the same email, call the number printed on the new invoice, or rush because the deadline is today.

entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: If something already happened
entries.text: If you entered credentials on a suspicious site, approved an unexpected MFA request, or opened an untrusted file, report it immediately using your organization's security process. Follow your IT team's incident instructions. If you suspect active malware or remote control, they may direct you to disconnect the affected device from the network. From a separate trusted device, change compromised passwords and revoke sessions as instructed. Preserve relevant messages and evidence. Key takeaway Early reporting helps your security team contain an incident. Do not wait until you are certain an attack succeeded.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona
Pretexting: the Fake Persona: By the end of this module you can:
entries.text: Explain how pretexting uses an invented identity and story to gain trust. Recognize fake auditors, vendors, HR representatives, and distressed coworkers. Notice attempts to bypass verification and official ticketing processes. Check unexpected data and access requests through established workplace channels. Helpful tip Click dotted-underlined terms for a quick explanation. Try “pretexting” above.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona: A believable story with a hidden goal
entries.text: Pretexting is a social engineering technique in which someone invents a situation and persona to persuade you to disclose information or grant access they are not authorized to receive.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona: Direct phishing
entries.text:
“Your account will close today. Click this link immediately.”
 Typical approach: a rapid request designed to trigger action.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona: Pretexting
entries.text:
“I'm helping with your team's onboarding review. Could I ask a few questions before we start?”
 Typical approach: a plausible role and story that can build trust over time.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona: How the story develops
entries.text: 1 Introduce a persona Claims to be an auditor, HR contact, or vendor. → 2 Build credibility Mentions real projects, people, or processes. → 3 Ask for access or data Requests records, credentials, or a process exception. Pretexting is not always slow. Some attempts happen in one conversation; others unfold over days. A detailed story or friendly tone does not establish authorization. Key takeaway Judge a request by independent verification and approved procedures, not by how believable the story sounds.

Spot the giveaways in a phishing email: a lookalike domain,

 — can slip past a Security Email Gateway ( SEG ) that mainly checks text links. Run the same three checks before clicking a link, scanning

entries.title: Phishing: In an office
entries.text:
In an office your computer sits behind a company firewall, an
 intrusion prevention system ( IPS ), and a monitored Security
 Email Gateway ( SEG ).

entries.title: Phishing: Working remotely
entries.text:
Working remotely, you connect straight to
 Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or Slack over home Wi-Fi, often
 on your own device ( BYOD ). None of that is in the way, so
 attacks arrive dressed as the tools you open daily.

entries.title: Phishing: Domain tricks
entries.text:
The fake sites lean on domain tricks. Typosquatting swaps one
 character: micros0ft.com for
 microsoft.com . Combosquatting adds
 trusted-sounding words, as in
 slack-login-security.net . When you open a website, you may see https:// and a padlock symbol in the address bar. This means your connection to that site is encrypted, not that the site belongs to a trustworthy company. Websites use SSL/TLS certificates to enable that encryption. And because an SSL/TLS certificate is free, the counterfeit server shows the same HTTPS padlock as the real one — which is what convinces people the login page is safe.

entries.title: Phishing: Domain tricks
entries.text:
Example of an official address https://www.microsoft.com Compare the domain with the company's known official website. Example of a fake address https://micros0ft-verify.com It also shows HTTPS, but the brand name contains a zero instead of the letter “o”. The padlock protects the connection; it does not verify who owns the website. Key takeaway 
 Lookalike website addresses can be difficult to notice. An HTTPS padlock alone does not prove a website is legitimate.

entries.title: Phishing: Quishing: the link inside a QR code
entries.text:
Imagine this: You receive an email that looks like it came from your company's HR or IT team. Instead of giving you a link, it tells you to scan a QR code using your phone to keep your account active. The code looks harmless, but you cannot tell where it leads just by looking at it. 1 Unexpected email “Scan to verify your account” 
 → 2 Personal phone The QR code opens a hidden web link 
 → 3 Fake sign-in A scammer tries to collect your password 
 Traditional phishing sends a clickable link the gateway can scan.

entries.title: Phishing: Quishing: the link inside a QR code
entries.text:
Quishing hides it in a QR code image that many gateways do not read,
 often opened on a personal phone with less protection. Many email filters mainly read text: the written HTML and any
 plain-text URL. Some newer gateways can run OCR (optical character
 recognition) or decode QR codes in images and PDF attachments,
 but many do not, and none catch every one. A Quick Response ( QR ) code is an image, so the link
 inside it can go unchecked. That is why quishing keeps
 growing against distributed staff.

entries.title: Phishing: Quishing: the link inside a QR code
entries.text:
The email claims to be an “ MFA Security Update” or
 an “HR Employee Handbook Review,” and the gateway
 may let it through. You scan it with your phone camera. The
 session moves off your work computer onto a personal phone
 that may not have the same protection, landing on a credential-harvesting 
 web form, or an OAuth page asking you to grant consent. In simple terms: Quishing is phishing with a QR code. A company email filter might inspect ordinary links, but it may not recognize a website address hidden inside a QR image.

entries.title: Phishing: Quishing: the link inside a QR code
entries.text:
Scanning with your personal phone can also move you away from the protections used on your work computer. The safest option is to open your company's official website yourself or confirm the request with your IT team. Key takeaway 
 QR codes can conceal links to fake login pages. Verify requests through an official channel before scanning.

entries.title: Phishing: Fear-based subject lines
entries.text:
Subject lines built on fear: “Urgent: Account
 Suspension in 2 Hours.” “Unusual Login Detected
 - Verify Immediately.”

entries.title: Phishing: Unsolicited QR code
entries.text:
An unsolicited QR code, to be scanned on your phone to
 reach a desktop web service.

entries.title: Phishing: Generic greeting or mismatched link
entries.text:
A greeting of “Dear Customer,” or link text
 reading portal.company.com that points at an
 unrelated IP address. Key takeaway 
 Watch for suspicious senders, urgent deadlines, unexpected QR
 codes, and links that do not match their stated destination.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages
Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: By the end of this module you can:
entries.text: Explain why smishing messages can feel trustworthy even when they are scams. Recognize spoofed sender IDs , shortened links, and fake portals. Spot fake delivery, bank, and digital-wallet alerts, including scams involving familiar apps and services. Protect your OTP and MFA codes, verify independently, and report suspicious messages. Helpful tip Click any highlighted, dotted-underlined term for a quick definition. Try “smishing” above.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: Why your phone can be the soft spot
entries.text: Smishing is phishing delivered through SMS or messaging apps such as WhatsApp, Viber, Signal, or Telegram. Attackers use messages to lure you into opening a harmful link, calling a fake support number, or revealing private information.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: SMS, email, and messaging apps
entries.text: The channel may change, but the trick is similar: impersonate someone you trust, create pressure, and ask you to act before checking. A phone's small screen may hide the full website address. Personal phones may also lack the same company security controls as managed laptops. Example: A freelancer receives a message claiming a GCash account needs urgent verification. The brand is familiar, but familiarity does not authenticate the message. Key takeaway A familiar app, sender name, or conversation thread does not guarantee that a message is legitimate.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: The everyday lures scammers use
entries.text: Scammers borrow situations you might encounter during a normal workday. Select each scenario to see the trap.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: {{ lure.title }}
Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: Hidden links and faked senders
entries.text: Shorteners such as bit.ly , tinyurl.com , and t.co can obscure a destination. A lookalike domain such as wallet-verify.example may imitate a real login portal. Sender ID spoofing can make a text appear to come from a trusted organization—even in an existing message thread on some networks. Important: A strange domain is a warning sign, but a familiar-looking domain or sender name alone is not proof of safety. Key takeaway Open your bank, wallet, courier, or employer's official app or bookmarked website yourself rather than following an unexpected message link.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: {{ flag.title }}
Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: What about the sender's number?
entries.text: A message from an unexpected ordinary mobile number claiming to be your bank or employer deserves caution. However, legitimate organizations can use different sender types, and scammers can spoof recognizable sender names. Never rely on the number or label alone. Key takeaway Urgency, unusual links, requests for codes, and sender inconsistencies are reasons to pause and verify.

Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: How to report a suspicious message
entries.text: Use your messaging app's report/block feature and notify your employer's IT or security team if work access is involved. In the Philippines, report scam texts through your network's official channel (such as Globe's #StopSpam page, or Smart or DITO customer support) or call the CICC anti-scam hotline 1326 . The 7726 (SPAM) shortcode used in some other countries is not the standard reporting number here, so follow your mobile provider's current scam-reporting guidance. If you already entered a password, shared an OTP, or approved an unexpected MFA request, contact the affected provider and your security team immediately using official channels.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research
Spear Phishing and Target Research: By the end of this module you can:
entries.text: Tell broad mass phishing apart from spear phishing written for one person or team. Recognize how open-source intelligence (OSINT) from LinkedIn, GitHub, and X can become a personalized lure. Spot the risk in a macro-enabled attachment, a double file extension, and a request to move to an out-of-band messaging channel. Helpful tip Click any highlighted, dotted-underlined term for a simple explanation. Try “spear phishing” above.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research: A message designed just for you
entries.text: Mass phishing sends thousands of similar messages, hoping someone clicks. Spear phishing targets a particular person, team, or organization using details that make a message feel familiar.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research: Spear phishing
entries.text:
“Hi Alex, can you review the Acme Corp proposal before our client call?”
 Approach: Uses your name, real work, and plausible timing to earn trust.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research: Why the familiar details matter
entries.text: An attacker might mention your current client engagement, a coworker's name, the platforms you use, or a recent company event. These details can be true even when the sender is an impostor. Imagine this: You receive a message apparently from a teammate at a conference. It references a real client and asks you to open an attachment. You recognize the project—but have you verified who actually sent it? Key takeaway Accurate personal details make a message believable; they do not prove it came from the claimed sender.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research: How attackers research a target
entries.text: OSINT means collecting information from publicly available sources. An attacker can combine small details into a convincing work-related request.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research: Putting the details together
entries.text:
Example: “Hi Alex, I'm at the TechSummit conference right now. Could you check the attached update for the Acme Corp project proposal? Password to unzip is 1234.”
 Names, conference attendance, and project details may all be real. The unexpected file and password still need independent verification. Key takeaway Information you post publicly can be combined into an impersonation attempt. Verify unusual requests using a trusted contact method.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research: Attachments that deserve a closer look
entries.text: A targeted message may carry a malicious file rather than a suspicious link. Select each example to learn what makes it risky.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research: {{ file.title }}
Spear Phishing and Target Research: Why password-protected archives matter
entries.text: Encrypted .zip , .rar , and .7z files may prevent some security scanners from inspecting their contents. A password included in the same unexpected email is not evidence that the file is safe. Key takeaway Don't enable unexpected macros, open disguised executable files, or extract unverified password-protected archives. Confirm the request before opening anything.

Vishing: Phishing by Phone: By the end of this module you can:
entries.text: Explain how caller ID spoofing and VoIP can make an unknown caller appear legitimate. Recognize how live conversations use urgency, authority, and pressure to influence decisions. Identify fake IT helpdesk calls, bank fraud alerts, and requests to install remote-access software. Protect your MFA approvals, verify callers independently, and report suspicious calls. Helpful tip Click highlighted, dotted-underlined terms to learn what they mean. Try “caller ID spoofing” above.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: What makes a phone call dangerous?
entries.text: Vishing is voice phishing: an attacker uses a phone call or internet-based voice service to trick someone into revealing sensitive information, transferring money, or granting access to a device.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: Vishing
entries.text: A caller responds immediately to your hesitation, adds pressure, and may discourage you from hanging up.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: {{ item.title }}
entries.text:
{{ item.description }}
 Imagine this: Your phone displays a familiar bank name. The caller claims your account is under attack and asks you to approve a login. Does the caller ID prove the call is real? Key takeaway A caller's name, number, or professional tone is not proof of identity. You can end the call and verify through a number you independently trust.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: The stories scammers use on calls
entries.text: A caller may use a familiar organization, an urgent problem, or an authoritative title to win your cooperation. Select a scenario to see the underlying tactic.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: {{ lure.title }}
Vishing: Phishing by Phone: Why live pressure works
entries.text: Manufactured urgency: “Your account will be locked in five minutes.” Borrowed authority: “I'm calling from IT Security.” No thinking room: “Stay on the line and do exactly what I say.” A skilled scammer may adapt their script based on your reaction. Key takeaway Urgency and authority are claims, not evidence. End the call before responding to an unexpected request involving money, codes, or device access.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: {{ flag.title }}
Vishing: Phishing by Phone: What if the caller ID looks correct?
entries.text: Caller ID spoofing can display a familiar number or name. Even a call appearing to come from a bank, coworker, or internal extension must be verified when it makes an unusual request. Key takeaway Requests for passwords, MFA approval, remote-control software, or immediate payment are reasons to hang up and independently verify.
