entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data: By the end of this module you can
entries.text: Explain why an instruction that appears to come from an executive is hard to question. Recognise a fake supervisor directive, including the urgent gift card or wire request. Spot password reset traps and single sign-on credential requests from an impersonated executive. Apply out-of-band (OOB) verification - confirming on a separate, already-trusted channel - to any high-stakes request, whatever rank it seems to come from.

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data: Why the assistant is the target
entries.text: A virtual assistant runs the executive calendar, books the travel, handles sensitive corporate mail, and often holds elevated access to cloud management portals. That makes the VA an administrative hub. Take their credentials, or just their trust, and you have indirect administrative access to the whole company (Lazarus, 2024).

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data: Authority and urgency
entries.text: A VA is expected to act on an executive request quickly. That responsiveness is the thing being exploited. The meeting excuse. A lookalike email address, or a WhatsApp or Telegram profile, carries the name of your CEO or CFO. They are locked in an all-day board meeting and cannot take calls, but they need an urgent task handled now. The story is built so you cannot phone to check. The purchase. Buy digital gift cards - Apple, Google Play, Amazon - or send an urgent wire, for a “client appreciation gift” or an “emergency vendor deposit.” Any delay, you are told, costs a multi-million dollar deal.

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data: Single sign-on and password reset traps
entries.text:
VAs often help with technical setup, so the same fake executive is used to get round the login controls. The reset. “I lost my phone and cannot receive my multi-factor push code. Contact IT, or use your admin access, and reset my password to TempPassword2026! immediately.”
 The push. The attacker logs into the executive’s real account, which sends repeated push notifications to your device. Then the call or text arrives: “Accept that notification on your screen right now - it’s me, logging in from the airport.”

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data: Scenario: the Friday afternoon emergency
entries.text: You are a remote virtual assistant at a tech startup. It is 4:30 PM on a Friday. A WhatsApp message arrives from a number showing the photo and name of your CEO, Sarah Jenkins.

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data: Stage 1 - the hook
entries.text:
“Hi! I’m in a closed-door meeting with investors. My laptop died and I can’t access Slack. Purchase 5 x $200 digital Apple gift cards right now for the investor team. Use the corporate card. Send the codes here ASAP. Do not call me, I’m presenting.”
 What do you do? A: Buy the gift cards on the corporate card, to impress the CEO and avoid ruining the investor meeting. B: Notice the familiar pattern - gift cards, urgency, no phone calls allowed - and pause. (Correct)

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data: Stage 2 - verifying
entries.text:
What is your next step? What do you do? A: Reply on WhatsApp: “Are you sure it’s you, Sarah?”
 B: Use an established internal channel - the CEO’s verified phone number, or a check with the Chief of Staff. (Correct)

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data: Red flags
entries.text: An executive asking you to buy digital gift cards or cryptocurrency, or to send an unverified wire. A message that tells you not to call, because they are in a meeting or on a flight. An executive turning up on personal WhatsApp or Telegram, or a non-corporate webmail address like ceo.company@gmail.com . Instructions to disable MFA, reset a password to a weak default, or share a login token over chat.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: By the end of this module you can
entries.text:
Recognise a fake client or job inquiry built to harvest credentials or get free work. Spot the portfolio trick, where a login is demanded before you can see the brief. Explain what you lose when a client moves you off-platform , away from escrow and contract cover. Verify a client out of band before you grant access or deliver work. Helpful tip
 Select any highlighted, dotted-underlined word to see a simple explanation. Try selecting “ credentials ” in the learning outcomes above! You’ll cover: Why freelancers get targeted Portfolio credential harvesting Getting you off the platform A real scenario Role-by-role practice 
 Use the menu to revisit a section.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: By the end of this module you can
entries.text: Mark each learning section reviewed when you are ready to continue. Practice questions do not replace the course assessment.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Why freelancers get targeted
entries.text:
A freelancer has no corporate IT perimeter , no in-house legal team and nobody doing security for them. Income depends on landing the next project, so the fear of losing a good one is always there. Attackers build a convincing “high-budget client” persona for exactly that reason: to make you drop your usual checks (Ticona, 2022). Key takeaway
 A promising project can make an unusual request feel reasonable. Keep the same verification routine even when the offer is attractive.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Portfolio credential harvesting
entries.text:
Not mass phishing. The pretext is a commercial brief written for you. 1 · The link “Review portal” link arrives 
 2 · The page Fake sign-in page 
 3 · You sign in You enter your account details 
 4 · Captured Password and MFA code taken 
 How a portfolio credential-harvesting attack unfolds. The review portal. A client interested in a high-value contract sends a link to a “prototype review portal” or “shared client workspace” - figma-client-verify.com , adobe-portfolio-review.site . Sign in with your professional account to see the brief, they say. The client’s own system.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Portfolio credential harvesting
entries.text:
You are asked to log into their staging server , CMS or cloud repository using credentials they supply. The login page is a harvester, built to capture your main password and your multi-factor code . Quick check: which address is the real Adobe domain? A: adobe.com 
 B: adobe-portfolio-review.site 
 C: adobe-client-login.net 
 Why a familiar logo is not enough
 A fake page can copy a logo, colors and layout. Open the service through your own bookmark or type its known address yourself. Treat the example addresses in this lesson as fictional simulations; do not visit them. Key takeaway
 A realistic brief can be bait.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Getting you off the platform
entries.text:
Upwork, Fiverr and Toptal log the contract, verify identities and hold payment in escrow . So the first move is to get you talking somewhere else. Understand the protection your arrangement provides
 Payment and dispute protections vary by platform and contract. Check your actual agreement. Moving to a different channel does not verify the client or establish that a payment is genuine. Within the agreed platform process
 Documented contract and messages
 Available identity checks
 Payment protections under the platform’s terms
 Pressure to bypass that process
 Unverified promises
 Reduced platform protection
 Requests for irreversible payments
 The convenience story.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Getting you off the platform
entries.text: Their accounting department cannot pay through the platform, and there is a 30% bonus if you accept a direct wire, PayPal Friends & Family, or cryptocurrency. The overpayment. An advance check or wire arrives for more than the agreed fee. An accounting error, they say - please return the difference now, by a method that cannot be reversed. The original payment is later flagged as fraudulent, leaving you owing what you refunded.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Getting you off the platform
entries.text:
1 · Advance Check or wire arrives 
 2 · Excess More than the agreed fee 
 3 · Pressure “Return the difference” 
 4 · Refund You send money by a one-way route 
 5 · Loss Original payment flagged as fraud 
 The overpayment, step by step: you end up owing what you refunded. Key takeaway
 Do not let a bonus or urgent start replace verification. If an unexpected overpayment arrives, contact your payment provider through its official channel before moving money.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Scenario: the high-retainer brand
entries.text: You are a freelance web developer. “Marcus Vance” emails you, says he is Marketing Director at an international agency, and offers a $12,000 retainer to redesign their core web platform. Fictional simulation. Choose a response at each stage to reveal feedback.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Stage 1 - first contact
entries.text: He sends a link to review the current environment and sitemap: nexus-agency-auth.net/sitemap . It opens a page identical to Google Workspace, asking you to log in with Google to view the protected brand assets. What do you do? A: Enter your Google credentials to see the sitemap and secure the $12,000 project. B: Enter nothing, look at the domain - nexus-agency-auth.net - and ask for the brief by email or as a PDF.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Stage 2 - the escrow bypass
Client Impersonation: More real-world scenarios
entries.text: Different jobs, similar tricks. Explore each role and choose what you would do. These are additional fictional practice examples. Designer Copywriter Marketing contractor Virtual assistant

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Designer — the review workspace
entries.text:
A “creative director” offers you a $2,500 brand refresh: “Sign in with Google to see our brief at portfolio-client-review.site/login .”
 What do you do? A: Sign in with Google. It is only to see the brief. B: Ask for the brief through the platform or as an attachment and verify the client out of band. C: Sign in, but use a throwaway password.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Copywriter — the unpaid launch
entries.text: A new client requests a complete campaign as a “quick sample” before agreeing a contract. They promise a long-term retainer if you deliver tonight. What do you do? A: Deliver the whole campaign to secure the retainer. B: Offer portfolio samples or a limited paid trial and agree the terms first.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Marketing contractor — urgent account access
entries.text: A supposed agency manager promises an advance but requests full administrator access to your client’s advertising account before any agreement is signed. What do you do? A: Grant full access so they can begin immediately. B: Verify the requester, obtain the account owner’s approval and limit permissions.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Virtual assistant — the excess advance
entries.text:
A new client sends more than the agreed advance. They ask you to return the difference immediately to another account, before the payment provider confirms the transfer. What do you do? A: Return the difference immediately to be helpful. B: Pause and contact your payment provider through its official channel. Key takeaway
 Whatever your role, watch for unnecessary logins, excessive access, work before agreed terms, and pressure to refund money before verification.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Red flags
entries.text:
A client who needs you to log into an unfamiliar third-party portal to read the spec or submit work. An early push to move the conversation, or the payment, off an escrow -protected platform. An advance for more than the agreed amount, with a request to refund the difference. A major agency writing from a lookalike domain or a free webmail account. Verify a client out of band
 Find the company’s official website yourself rather than following a link in the message. Contact the company through independently found details to confirm the person and project. Compare the sender’s full domain with the official company domain.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Red flags
entries.text:
Confirm the scope, contract and payment arrangement through the platform’s own messages and records. Replying “Are you real?” to the same email or calling a number supplied in it does not provide independent verification. Quick check: which action verifies the client independently? A: Reply to their email and ask, “Are you real?” 
 B: Find the company’s official website yourself and contact the company using details listed there. C: Call the phone number in the email signature they sent you. Do’s and don’ts
 Do
 Verify through a separate trusted channel. Keep a record of agreed scope and payment. Grant only necessary, authorized access. Don’t
 Share your password or MFA code.

entries.title: Client Impersonation: Red flags
entries.text:
Let urgency replace checks. Refund an unexpected excess payment under pressure. Module key takeaways
 A high-value offer does not establish identity. Read the full domain before signing in. Verify independently before granting access or delivering work. Keep agreed contract and payment protections in place. Ask your payment provider about unexpected overpayments before acting.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers
entries.text: Who this is for: remote job seekers, freelancers between contracts, contract workers, and remote HR coordinators.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers: By the end of this module you can
entries.text: Explain how fake outreach, fake postings and counterfeit contracts fit together. Recognise PII harvesting dressed up as a background check or onboarding. Explain the fake equipment check scam aimed at new remote hires. Verify a recruiter’s identity, their corporate domain and the contract before sharing personal records.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers: Why remote hiring is easy to fake
entries.text: Remote hiring opened up global recruiting, and recruitment fraud with it. Resumes, contact details and career histories sit in public on LinkedIn, Indeed and Upwork. Attackers harvest that and build an offer shaped around what you are hoping to earn (Ravenelle et al., 2022).

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers: Fake recruiters and PII harvesting
entries.text: The profile is either invented or copied from a real talent acquisition specialist at a company you have heard of. The text-only interview. An email or message offers an interview for a well-paid, fully remote role. It runs entirely in Telegram, Signal or Google Chat, or an automated questionnaire. No voice, no video. The onboarding forms. With the “job offer” comes a demand for personally identifiable information (PII): passport scans, government ID numbers, bank account details for direct deposit, your social security number - all for the “pre-employment background check” or “tax form processing.” The data goes straight to identity theft and financial fraud (Anbarasu et al., 2024).

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers: The fake equipment check
entries.text: A widespread scam aimed at new remote hires. It turns on how long a bank takes to clear a check. A counterfeit check arrives - say $3,500 - to buy home office equipment: laptop, monitors, an ergonomic desk. You are told to deposit it in your personal account and wire the money straight on to a “certified vendor,” which is them. Days later the bank finds the check is fraudulent and reverses the $3,500. You are out the money you wired, and your account may be closed for depositing a fake check.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers: Scenario: the exclusive coordinator offer
entries.text: You have been applying for remote roles online. An email from careers@tech-global-corp.net offers you a “Remote Operations Coordinator” post at $95,000 a year.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers: Stage 1 - the interview
entries.text: The recruiter, “David Miller,” writes: “Congratulations! Our board selected you from your resume. No video interview required - just complete the attached employment contract and background form.” Onboarding_Form.pdf asks for your full government ID number, a passport scan, and your bank account credentials. What do you do? A: Complete the form and attach the passport scan to secure the $95,000 offer. B: Pause and investigate. An offer with no video or voice interview that demands your bank login is a major fraud indicator. (Correct)

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers: Stage 2 - the equipment check
entries.text:
David Miller messages: “We are mailing you a check for $4,000. Deposit it and wire $3,200 to our approved hardware supplier via Zelle today.”
 What do you do? A: Deposit the check and wire the $3,200 now, so your work laptop arrives. B: Refuse the check, report the posting as fraudulent, and wire none of your own money. (Correct)

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers: Red flags
entries.text: An offer made without a single live video or voice interview. A check sent in advance to buy equipment from a named “approved vendor” by irreversible wire. A request for your bank account password or full tax ID before any contract is signed. A hiring address on a domain that is not the company’s own - @company-careers-jobs.com instead of @company.com .

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams
entries.text: Who this is for: remote bookkeepers, finance coordinators, payroll assistants, account managers, and small-business operations staff.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams: By the end of this module you can
entries.text: Explain how business email compromise works when finance runs over email. Spot a changed bank detail on a real invoice, and a lookalike sender domain. Recognise a payroll redirect request for what it is. Apply out-of-band verification and dual approval before money moves.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams: Business email compromise
entries.text: Business email compromise is the costliest form of social engineering. When finance runs over email, an attacker does not need to break anything - they only need one convincing message. Using a compromised mailbox or a spoofed domain, they redirect a payment you were always going to make (Lazarus, 2024).

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams: Changed bank details on a real invoice
entries.text: The usual route into a remote finance team. The invoice is genuine; only the account number is not. The access. The attacker gets into a vendor's mailbox, or registers a near-identical domain - vendor-supplies.co for vendor-supplies.com . The request. An invoice arrives for a contract you really do have, with a line saying the banking details have changed after an audit, and to pay the new account. Why it works. The formatting, the project name and the contact history all match your records, so there is nothing obvious to doubt (Papathanasiou et al., 2023).

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams: Payroll redirect
entries.text: The same trick aimed at HR instead of accounts payable. A message that looks like it is from a colleague: they have changed banks, please update the direct deposit before Friday. It lands just before the payroll deadline, so there is no time to check. Updated without a second check, that person's pay goes to the attacker.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams: The two controls that stop it
entries.text: Verify out of band. Never change bank details from an email alone. Call the number on the signed contract - not the one on the new invoice. Require two people. Above an agreed amount, one person raises the payment and a second approves it. Read the headers. The displayed sender and the actual sending server often disagree. That gap is the tell.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams: Scenario: the annual renewal
entries.text: You handle accounts payable for a software firm. An email arrives from billing@cloud-hosting-services.co . Your provider's real domain is cloud-hosting-services.com .

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams: Stage 1 - the request
entries.text:
“Attached is Invoice #8841 for your annual cloud hosting renewal ($14,500). Our bank details have changed. Please wire to our new account at First Global Bank.”
 What do you do? A: Update the vendor record and send the $14,500 now, to avoid the servers going down. B: Notice .co is not .com , hold the payment, and verify. (Correct)

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams: Stage 2 - verifying
entries.text: You decide to confirm the new account by phone. Which number? What do you do? A: The number printed at the bottom of the new invoice. B: The account manager's number from your signed contract. (Correct)

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams: Red flags
entries.text: A bank detail change requested just before a payment or payroll deadline. A sender domain that is one character off the real one. A push to switch payment method - to a wire, Zelle, or gift cards. A payroll change sent from someone's personal webmail.

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data
entries.text: Why do cybercriminals frequently target Virtual Assistants (VAs) in executive impersonation attacks? VAs hold central administrative access and high-level trust, making them high-value targets (Lazarus, 2024).

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data
entries.text: An email from a CEO requesting that a Virtual Assistant purchase $1,000 in Apple gift cards for a "client emergency" is almost certainly a social engineering scam. Requesting gift card purchases is a primary financial scam tactic; legitimate businesses do not use gift cards for emergency corporate transactions.

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data
entries.text: You receive a message on Telegram from your remote boss: "I am on a plane with no voice signal. Send me the MFA code that was just sent to your phone so I can access my email." What should you do? MFA tokens grant account access and must never be shared, even if the requester claims to be an executive.

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data
entries.text: Which of the following elements are red flags indicative of executive impersonation? (Select TWO) Prohibiting voice verification and using external webmail accounts are classic executive spoofing indicators.

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data
entries.text: Threat actors use psychological authority pressure to make Virtual Assistants feel that questioning an executive's request will lead to immediate firing. Fear of disciplinary action is manipulated to force VAs to bypass security checks.

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data
entries.text: What is "Out-of-Band (OOB) Verification" in the context of Virtual Assistant workflows? OOB verification confirms identity via a separate, trusted channel (e.g., calling a known phone number).

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data
entries.text: You manage the calendar for a remote Vice President. An external consultant emails asking you to add a Zoom link to the VP's calendar for a "confidential acquisition meeting." The email attachment is Meeting_Agenda.docm. What should you do? Unsolicited macro-enabled files (.docm) are common malware delivery vectors.

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data
entries.text: What term describes an attacker flooding a Virtual Assistant's phone with dozens of login push notifications late at night in hopes the VA will tap "Approve"? MFA fatigue exploits distraction and frustration to coerce push approvals.

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data
entries.text: If an executive texts you from a new, unverified phone number claiming they lost their device, you should immediately grant them full access to all company cloud drives without secondary verification. Identity must be independently verified through official channels before granting access from new devices.

entries.title: Executive Impersonation and Client Data
entries.text: Why do pretexters impersonating executives create artificial time emergencies ("Need this done in 15 minutes before board meeting")? Artificial time pressure suppresses analytical thinking and security protocol adherence.

entries.title: Client Impersonation
entries.text: Why are independent freelancers particularly attractive targets for social engineering scams? Income unpredictability and isolation from corporate IT oversight increase vulnerability to fake client lures (Ticona, 2022).

entries.title: Client Impersonation
entries.text: A client demanding that you log into a third-party website using your personal Google or Microsoft credentials to view a project brief is a major indicator of portfolio credential harvesting. Legitimate project briefs do not require logging in with personal OAuth credentials on unverified third-party domains.

entries.title: Client Impersonation
entries.text: A prospective client offers you a $5,000 project but insists on moving communications off Upwork to Telegram before a contract is started. They offer to pay via an unverified check. What should you do? Luring freelancers off-platform removes contract enforcement and escrow protections, exposing them to payment fraud.

entries.title: Client Impersonation
entries.text: Which of the following indicate that an incoming freelance inquiry is a social engineering scam? (Select TWO) Overpayment refund demands and premature requests for administrative server credentials are key fraud indicators.

entries.title: Client Impersonation
entries.text: Escrow services on freelance platforms protect freelancers by holding client funds in a neutral account until agreed project milestones are met. Escrow ensures funds are verified and set aside before work begins, reducing non-payment risks.

entries.title: Client Impersonation
entries.text: What is the primary objective of a "Portfolio Credential Harvesting" attack targeting freelancers? Fake login portals capture credentials to compromise professional accounts and cloud repositories.

entries.title: Client Impersonation
entries.text: You receive a $2,000 advance payment check from a new client. Two days later, the client emails: "Our accountant made a mistake and sent $3,500. Please Zelle us back the $1,500 difference right away." What is the safest course of action? Fake check overpayment scams rely on the victim wiring real money before the bank discovers the deposited check is counterfeit.

entries.title: Client Impersonation
entries.text: Which domain name is a combosquatted lookalike designed to trick a freelancer using Figma for client design reviews? figma-verify-review.net is combosquatting: it adds trusted-sounding words to the Figma brand on a domain Figma does not own, to capture your login. The other three are real Figma addresses. Typosquatting is different: it changes a character, such as figrna.com.

entries.title: Client Impersonation
entries.text: Legitimate corporate clients will routinely ask freelancers to purchase gift cards as part of their initial onboarding duties. Requesting gift card purchases during onboarding is a classic financial scam.

entries.title: Client Impersonation
entries.text: What should a freelancer do before opening a zip file sent by a new, unverified client? Unverified attachments can contain malicious scripts or executable payloads.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers
entries.text: What is the primary goal of scammers running fake remote job outreach campaigns? Fake job scams harvest PII and run advance-fee equipment check schemes (Ravenelle et al., 2022).

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers
entries.text: A legitimate international company will routinely hire remote employees for high-paying roles based purely on a 10-minute text conversation on Telegram without any video or voice interviews. Text-only "interviews" on anonymous messaging apps are major indicators of recruitment fraud.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers
entries.text: You are hired for a remote position. The company mails you a $3,000 check and instructs you to deposit it, keep $500 as a sign-on bonus, and wire $2,500 to an "approved software vendor." What should you do? Fake check scams rely on victims wiring real money before the bank identifies the deposited check as fraudulent.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers
entries.text: Which of the following details indicate that a remote job offer may be fraudulent? (Select TWO) Requesting bank passwords and using lookalike email domains indicate recruitment fraud.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers
entries.text: Legitimate employers require new hires to pay application fees or background check fees upfront via cryptocurrency. Legitimate employers cover hiring and background check costs; demanding crypto payments indicates fraud.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers
entries.text: What type of sensitive data is targeted during pre-employment PII harvesting scams? PII is harvested to commit identity theft, open fraudulent credit lines, or breach accounts.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers
entries.text: You receive an email from hr@microsoft-remote-careers.site inviting you to apply for an administrative position. How can you verify if this domain belongs to Microsoft? Always cross-reference job outreach domains against official corporate career portals.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers
entries.text: How does the fake equipment check scam operate? The counterfeit check bounces after the victim has already transferred real personal funds to the scammer.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers
entries.text: Scammers frequently copy authentic logos, employee photos, and executive names from LinkedIn to create convincing fake recruiter profiles. Copied branding assets build false credibility and lower applicant vigilance.

entries.title: Fake Job and Recruiter Offers
entries.text: What is the primary risk of uploading your full unredacted driver's license or passport scan to an unverified job portal? Unredacted government IDs are primary assets used in identity fraud and unauthorized account creation.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams
entries.text: What is the primary objective of a Business Email Compromise (BEC) attack targeting remote finance workers? BEC targets financial communications to divert payments to fraudulent accounts (Lazarus, 2024).

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams
entries.text: An email requesting an urgent update to a vendor's bank account details should always be verified by calling a phone number from the original master contract. Out-of-band verification using known contract phone numbers prevents invoice manipulation fraud.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams
entries.text: A remote employee emails HR from john.smith-work@gmail.com asking to change their direct deposit bank account before Friday's payroll. What should HR do? Direct deposit changes sent via personal email accounts are primary targets for payroll interception.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams
entries.text: Which of the following indicate that an invoice update request may be a BEC attempt? (Select TWO) Typosquatted domains and extreme artificial time pressure are indicators of BEC fraud.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams
entries.text: Calling the phone number listed on a suspicious new invoice is a safe way to verify if the invoice's bank account changes are real. If the invoice is fake, the phone number on it leads directly to the scammer. Use trusted numbers from master contracts.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams
entries.text: What internal financial control requires two separate individuals to review and approve wire transfers above a designated threshold? Dual-custody ensures that a single manipulated employee cannot execute unauthorized transfers alone.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams
entries.text: A long-time vendor emails an invoice for $22,000. The invoice matches the expected amount, but a note says: "Our bank is undergoing an audit. Wire payment to our new overseas account." What is the safest response? Audit excuses for sudden overseas account changes are common BEC pretexts requiring verification.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams
entries.text: In an email header, what field shows the actual mail server that sent the message, helping reveal domain spoofing? Email headers reveal true server origins, exposing sender address spoofing.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams
entries.text: Business Email Compromise (BEC) attacks only use fake domains; they never involve real, compromised vendor email accounts. Attackers frequently compromise real vendor accounts (Vendor Email Compromise) to send fraudulent invoices from actual mailboxes.

entries.title: Invoice and Payment Scams
entries.text: Why do BEC scammers target remote finance workers right before weekends or major holidays? Rushing before deadlines reduces vigilance, increasing the likelihood that security protocols will be skipped.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: The presence of "HTTPS" and a padlock icon in the browser address bar guarantees that a login website is legitimate and safe. False. Threat actors can easily acquire free SSL/TLS certificates for fraudulent domain names, displaying HTTPS padlock icons on malicious credential-harvesting websites.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: Which domain name represents an example of "typosquatting"? login.micros0ft.com uses a zero ('0') in place of the letter 'o' so it looks like Microsoft at a glance. The other three are real domains that belong to Google, Microsoft and Slack.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: What is the primary objective of an email phishing attack targeting remote employees? Email phishing uses deceptive messages to trick victims into sharing private credentials, executing malware, or surrendering sensitive organizational data.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: Why do quishing attacks often succeed when targeting remote employees? Scanning QR codes on personal phones redirects traffic outside the desktop perimeter firewalls and email monitoring systems maintained by corporate networks.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: You receive an email notification stating your company cloud portal requires urgent re-authentication, with a link included. What is the safest way to access the portal? Navigating independently via a trusted bookmark or manual URL entry completely bypasses any malicious redirects embedded in the email.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: When an unexpected email asks you to verify an account, the lesson recommends opening the official site independently rather than following the message link. The lesson recommends using a trusted bookmark or entering the official address yourself instead of following an unexpected email link.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: A QR code from an unexpected vendor document opens a familiar sign-in or OAuth page. Is the familiar sign-in brand alone enough reason to proceed without verifying the request? A QR code can conceal the destination of a link. Verify an unexpected request through a trusted channel before entering credentials or granting access.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: A suspicious link uses slack-login-security.net while claiming to be the Slack sign-in page. Which domain trick does this example illustrate? Combosquatting adds trusted-sounding words to a familiar brand name. The lesson uses slack-login-security.net as its example.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: You receive an unexpected email asking you to sign in through an included link to view a security update. How should you check the request? The lesson recommends opening the official site independently or confirming an unexpected request through a known official channel.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: You realize you entered your password on a fake login page. Which actions are taught in this lesson? (Select ALL that apply) The lesson advises reporting the incident and changing reused passwords. Clearing local browser history does not address a password already entered on a fake page.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: What does the term "Quishing" refer to in modern cybersecurity? Quishing stands for QR code phishing. The malicious link is placed inside an image, which can get past email filters that mainly check text links.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: Security Email Gateways (SEGs) detect embedded QR code links just as easily as standard plain-text web links. False. Many email gateways mainly check text and HTML links. A QR code is an image, so its link can slip past filters that do not decode images. Some newer gateways can read QR codes, but none catch every one, so treat unexpected QR codes with caution.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: Which of the following indicators strongly suggest that an email may be a phishing attempt? (Select ALL that apply) The lesson identifies sender and domain mismatches, urgency, and QR codes that conceal links as reasons to verify an unexpected message.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: You receive an email from IT-Support@company-desk.net stating: "Your password expires in 10 minutes. Click here to retain your current password." What should you do first? You should pause and verify unrequested urgent security alerts independently through official internal channels.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: Which observations match the domain and QR-code warning signs taught in this lesson? (Select ALL that apply) The lesson shows typosquatting (micros0ft.com swaps the letter o for a zero), combosquatting (slack-login-security.net adds trusted-sounding words to a brand), and QR codes that hide where they lead. HTTPS means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is genuine.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: A QR code in an unexpected document is labeled "View client agreement" and opens a sign-in page. Is the label alone enough reason to enter your credentials? A QR code can hide its destination. Verify the unexpected request with a trusted contact before entering credentials.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: Combosquatting involves adding words like "-security" or "-login" to legitimate brand names within a domain registration. True. Combosquatting merges legitimate brand trademarks with keywords (e.g., paypal-update-center.com) to mislead recipients.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: Which statements about an HTTPS padlock are accurate according to the lesson? (Select ALL that apply) The lesson explains that HTTPS protects the connection, but free SSL/TLS certificates mean a counterfeit site can display the same padlock.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: Why do attackers create urgency in a phishing message? The lesson explains that urgent deadlines pressure recipients to act before checking the request independently.

entries.title: Phishing
entries.text: This lesson shows that phishing can use deceptive emails and websites as well as QR codes that hide links; it is not limited to business email. The lesson covers deceptive email and website requests and explains how QR codes can conceal links to fake login pages.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: How does spear phishing differ from generic mass phishing? Spear phishing relies on prior reconnaissance to tailor realistic messages directly to specific targets.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: Public professional profiles on LinkedIn can provide attackers with information used to craft spear phishing messages. True. Attackers mine job titles, reporting structures, vendor software, and current projects from LinkedIn profiles to build convincing pretexts.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: A vendor you've never worked with emails you a password-protected .zip file labeled "Invoice_Overdue.zip" and asks you to enter the password from a separate message to open it. Why might an attacker package a malicious attachment this way? Email gateway scanners cannot inspect encrypted archive contents without the password, allowing malicious payloads past boundary defenses.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: Which public sources are commonly harvested by adversaries during the OSINT phase of a spear phishing campaign? (Select ALL that apply) LinkedIn, GitHub, and social media posts provide open public data. Private encrypted database servers are not public OSINT sources.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: Spear phishing can target remote staff based on their system access, administrative privileges, financial responsibilities, or public profile; it is not limited to executives. The lesson identifies remote staff with system access, administrative privileges, financial responsibilities, or public profiles as its audience.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: Public details on LinkedIn, GitHub, or social media can be combined to personalize a spear-phishing lure. The lesson explains that attackers combine publicly available profile, project, and social-media details to make a lure more personal.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: An email claiming to be from your company's HR department contains a link to “Updated W-2 Tax Forms.” The link URL points to an external domain unrelated to your company. What is the safest course of action? The lesson recommends verifying unusual requests independently through a trusted contact method rather than relying on a message link.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: Spear phishing relies solely on technical software exploits and does not use psychological manipulation. Spear phishing is a socio-technical attack combining technical delivery vectors with psychological manipulation (trust, urgency, authority).

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: What should you do before opening an unexpected password-protected archive from an external party? The lesson warns that password-protected archives may be difficult for scanners to inspect and says to confirm unexpected requests before opening attachments.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: An attacker researching you before sending a spear-phishing email finds your public GitHub profile. What information could they gather there to make their message more believable? The lesson's GitHub example covers public projects, repositories, programming frameworks, and technologies.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: What does the acronym "OSINT" stand for in cybersecurity reconnaissance? OSINT stands for Open Source Intelligence, referring to publicly available data mined from social platforms, repositories, and directories.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: Enabling macros on an unverified Microsoft Word or Excel attachment is safe as long as the document has a .docm extension. False. The .docm extension explicitly denotes a macro-enabled document. Enabling macros runs underlying VBA code that can install malware.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: You are a remote graphic designer. You receive a direct message on Telegram from someone claiming to be a senior manager at your main client account, asking you to open Design_Brief.pdf.exe. How should you react? Files ending in .exe are executable programs. The .pdf.exe naming convention tricks users into opening executable malware.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: A message that mentions a real project or travel detail is safe to trust because the detail is accurate. Public information can make a spear-phishing lure convincing. The lesson advises verifying unusual requests using a trusted contact method.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: Which practices match the attachment-safety guidance taught in this lesson? (Select ALL that apply) The lesson warns about disguised double extensions and unexpected macros and recommends confirming unexpected files through a trusted channel.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: A spear phisher notices on Twitter that your company’s Lead Developer is on a 14-hour flight. The attacker emails you posing as the Lead Developer, requesting emergency production database credentials. Should you comply? False. Attackers exploit travel schedules to create situations where the spoofed identity cannot be reached easily. Always follow established verification protocols.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: An unexpected attachment asks you to enable macros before you can read it. What should you do? The lesson says not to enable unexpected macros and to confirm an unexpected attachment with the sender before opening it.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: Which attachment clues match risks taught in this lesson? (Select TWO) The lesson specifically warns about disguised double extensions and unexpected macro-enabled Office files.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: A freelancer receives an unexpected file named Project_Brief.pdf.exe and is urged to open it immediately. What makes this attachment suspicious? The lesson uses names such as report.pdf.exe to show how a double extension can disguise an executable as a document.

entries.title: Spear Phishing
entries.text: An email claims to be from HR, but its sender address uses an unrelated external domain. What should you do? The lesson teaches independent verification of unusual requests and warns that a message's apparent identity does not make its request trustworthy.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: You receive a text message from an unknown number containing a suspicious link and urging you to act immediately. What is the safest action to take? Refraining from interaction and deleting/reporting the message mitigates risk.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: You receive an unexpected text in a familiar bank-message thread. Does the existing thread or familiar sender ID prove that the new text is genuine? Sender IDs can be spoofed, including in an existing message thread. Verify an unexpected request using the bank's official app, website, or published phone number.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: What does the term "Smishing" stand for? Smishing combines "SMS" (text messaging) and "phishing".

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: You receive a text message: "USPS Alert: Your package cannot be delivered due to an incorrect house number. Update info here: bit.ly/3xY9zQ". You are expecting a package. What is the correct action? Always verify parcel delivery alerts by accessing the official website or app independently, never through unsolicited SMS links.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: You should never send a one-time verification code to someone who asks for it in a text message. The lesson says verification codes protect accounts and should not be shared with someone who asks for them.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: You receive a smishing text on your Philippine mobile number. What is the best way to report it? Report scam texts through your mobile network's official spam reporting channel or the CICC anti-scam hotline 1326, then block the sender. Replying or calling back confirms your number is active, and forwarding the text spreads the scam. The 7726 (SPAM) shortcode used in some other countries is not the standard reporting number in the Philippines.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: An unknown WhatsApp contact claims to be from your company's IT team and sends an unexpected work-access link. How should you respond? The lesson advises verifying unexpected work-access messages through known work channels instead of following unsolicited links.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: An attacker may trigger a real one-time code and then send a text asking you to share that code. The lesson's OTP-grab example explains that an attacker can trigger a real code and then ask the recipient to send it.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: You attempt to log into your work portal. A minute later, you receive a text: "IT Helpdesk: We detected an abnormal login. Reply YES with the code you just received to block the login." What is happening? Attackers trigger a real login prompt to generate a genuine OTP, then smish the victim to forward that OTP to complete the breach.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: What technology allows scammers to change the phone number or name displayed on your mobile incoming text screen? Sender ID spoofing allows SMS gateways to modify the header sender text displayed on receiver phones.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: If a text message appears in the same chat thread as previous legitimate bank messages, it is 100% guaranteed to be safe. Attackers can use Sender ID spoofing to inject fake text messages into existing SMS conversation threads on mobile devices.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: Why are mobile browsers particularly vulnerable to web link deceptive techniques? Reduced screen size makes it difficult for users to inspect the full domain path of a link before interacting.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: Which of the following are primary indicators of a smishing attempt? *(Select TWO)* The lesson shows a fake parcel-delivery text with a shortened link and warns never to share an MFA code requested by text.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: What is the risk of using shortened URLs (bit.ly, tinyurl) in SMS messages? URL shorteners hide the real destination address, concealing malicious domains.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: Personal smartphones used under BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) policies are always protected by corporate firewalls. Personal BYOD phones usually connect through mobile data or home Wi-Fi, so traffic does not pass through the office firewall. Unless the company manages the phone (for example with mobile device management or a VPN), it may not have the same protection as a work laptop.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: A remote worker receives a text message: *"HR ALERT: Update your direct deposit bank details at* *https://payroll-portal-update.com* *before 5 PM to receive this week's paycheck."* What should the worker check first? Urgent threats regarding payroll/direct deposit sent via text require out-of-band verification.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: What should you do if a text asks you to provide a one-time code for a work account? The lesson warns not to share one-time codes and recommends checking unexpected work-account requests through trusted channels.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: A text message reads: *"Bank Alert: Fraud detected. Call 1-800-555-0199 immediately to cancel the transaction."* What is the safest way to call your bank? The lesson recommends verifying a bank alert through a published number or the bank's official site rather than relying on contact details in an unexpected text.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: Which TWO risks can make a smishing link harder to assess on a personal phone than on a company-managed laptop? The lesson notes that personal phones may have less web filtering or endpoint protection, and that small screens or in-app browsers can make destinations harder to inspect.

entries.title: Smishing
entries.text: Legitimate logistics companies will always require you to pay a re-delivery fee via a third-party link sent by SMS. Demanding credit card details via SMS links for "unclaimed parcels" is a standard smishing lure.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: A caller can make a call display a different name or number from their actual identity. The lesson explains that caller ID can display a familiar name or number even when the caller is an impostor.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: An unknown caller on the phone becomes aggressive and demands that you immediately verify your account details over the call. What is the best immediate response? Aggressive emotional pressure is a hallmark of vishing; hanging up terminates the attack vector.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: Official company helpdesks frequently call remote workers unannounced to demand their personal email passwords. Legitimate helpdesks do not require your private account passwords to perform administrative tasks.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: While on a call with someone claiming to be from IT, you accidentally approve an MFA prompt they triggered. What should you do next? The lesson teaches ending unexpected calls and reporting suspicious requests through trusted organizational channels.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: An official bank representative will hang up on you if you state that you are hanging up to call back via the number on your payment card. Legitimate representatives encourage safe verification habits and welcome callbacks to official lines.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: Scammers can imitate an automated bank phone menu, such as a prompt to press 1 for support. The lesson explains that scammers can imitate automated phone menus and bank-call experiences.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: If an unexpected caller's identity or caller ID seems familiar, you should still verify unusual requests using a number you independently trust. The lesson explains that caller ID can be spoofed and recommends independently verifying unusual requests.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: An incoming call displays your bank's exact toll-free phone number. The caller states: "Security Alert: A $900 transfer was attempted. Read the code we just sent your phone to cancel it." What should you do? Spoofed Caller ID makes fake calls appear genuine; hanging up and calling back independently confirms authenticity.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: A caller claims to be from your bank and asks for a one-time code to stop a suspicious transfer. What is the safest response? The lesson's bank-call example warns not to share a verification code and recommends independently contacting the bank through an official number.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: Which of the following information should you NEVER read aloud or share during an inbound phone call? (Select TWO) Passwords and OTPs must remain confidential and should never be disclosed over inbound calls.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: What is "Vishing"? Vishing is social engineering delivered via voice/phone communication.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: You receive a call from "Corporate IT Support" stating your laptop is infected. The caller instructs you to go to a website and install AnyDesk so they can clean the machine. What should you do? Installing remote desktop software on unsolicited calls gives attackers full control over your endpoint.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: Which vishing tactic can pressure a target to act before verifying an unexpected request? The lesson describes callers using real-time pressure by interrupting questions and insisting on immediate action.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: What term describes repeated MFA prompts that may pressure a user into approving an attacker’s sign-in? MFA fatigue uses repeated prompts, sometimes paired with a convincing call, to pressure a user into approving an attacker’s sign-in.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: What is the primary objective of a vishing attacker who convinces a remote employee to install Quick Assist or TeamViewer? The lesson explains that remote-access software can let another person view or control a device; use it only after verifying an approved IT request.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: Vishing can occur through internet-based voice services, not only traditional phone lines. The lesson explains that attackers may misuse internet-based voice services (VoIP) to impersonate trusted callers.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: Which technique helps mitigate the risk of Caller ID spoofing when receiving unexpected internal calls? Calling back via a independently verified number bypasses spoofed inbound routing.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: An unexpected caller claims to be an executive and urgently asks you to provide a one-time code to resolve an account problem. What red flag is present? The lesson identifies authority and urgency as pressure tactics and warns callers may request MFA approval or codes.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: Which department should a remote employee contact to report a suspicious vishing call impersonating internal staff? Security teams handle threat logging, account isolation, and incident analysis.

entries.title: Vishing
entries.text: Which of the following indicators suggest an incoming phone call is a vishing attempt? *(Select TWO)* Emergency protocol bypasses and requests for passcodes are primary vishing tactics.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: A pretext may use a believable identity or story and rely on trust, empathy, or authority to persuade someone. The lesson says believable stories and personas can exploit trust, empathy, authority, and urgency to gain cooperation.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: A caller you don't recognize asks you to send over sensitive corporate information, claiming it's urgently needed for a same-day audit. What is the gold standard rule for handling this kind of request? Always verify identity and clearance before transmitting sensitive data.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: How do identity verification and documented procedures help reduce the risk of pretexting? The lesson teaches that verification and approved channels add checks that help protect confidential information; they do not guarantee that every pretext will be prevented.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: What distinguishes a pretext from a direct request that simply asks for information or access? The lesson defines pretexting as using a false identity or convincing story to gain trust and obtain information or access.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: How can an invented identity or story help a pretexter? The lesson explains that a false identity or believable story can gain trust before an attacker asks for sensitive information or access.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: Someone posing as a vendor pressures you to resolve their "urgent" access request directly with them instead of submitting an official IT service ticket. Why might a pretexter want to avoid the formal ticketing process? The lesson says urgency does not replace identity checks or documented approval; use the established process or an authorized exception path.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: The lesson's examples include remote administrators and workers handling HR, customer, or vendor information, not only executives. The lesson identifies remote workers handling administrative data, HR workflows, customer records, and vendor management as its audience.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: A new vendor asks for a sample customer export to test its system, but Procurement has not confirmed the contract. What should you do? The lesson's new-vendor example says to confirm the contract and approved data-sharing scope because even sample files may contain sensitive information.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: Out-of-band verification is ineffective against pretexting. Independent out-of-band verification effectively exposes pretexts by contacting the real organization or individual.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: A WhatsApp message from a new number claims to be a coworker who lost a phone and urgently asks you to forward a customer spreadsheet. What should you do? The lesson's coworker example uses an unknown WhatsApp number and a request for customer records; verify the person's identity through established work channels before sharing records.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: What is the primary characteristic of a pretexting attack? Pretexting centers on creating a plausible false persona and narrative.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: Pretexting attacks always happen within a single 30-second interaction and never involve multi-day conversations. Pretexting often uses a "slow-burn" approach, building rapport across multiple days or weeks.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: An external auditor asks for an employee directory or software inventory and says an IT ticket will take too long. What should the worker do? The lesson's process-bypass guidance says to verify identity and authorization and not skip documented approval for an external request.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: Which of the following personas are common disguises used in pretexting campaigns? *(Select TWO)* The lesson describes an external auditor requesting an employee directory and software inventory, and a new-vendor persona requesting a sample customer export before Procurement confirms the contract.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: A LinkedIn message claims to be from HR and uses a plausible job title. Does that alone prove the sender is genuine? The lesson's fictional LinkedIn HR example shows that a plausible title and friendly conversation do not verify identity or authorization.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: A pretext begins with casual conversation over several days before the attacker makes an unusual request. What is the attacker building during that time? The lesson explains that a pretext can build trust over time or unfold across days, but a friendly tone does not establish authorization.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: A remote contractor receives an email from someone claiming to be "Head of Global Security": *"We are running a silent security exercise. Do not inform your supervisor. Send your current VPN credentials directly to this email."* What should the contractor do? Demands for secrecy and credential submission are major red flags; legitimate security exercises do not collect user passwords via email.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: Which conversational signs suggest an interaction may be a pretexting attempt? *(Select TWO)* Bypassing procedures and using high-emotion stories are common pretexting tactics.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: An external auditor asks for employee home addresses. What should you do? The lesson treats employee records as sensitive and directs workers to verify requests through established HR and approval channels.

entries.title: Pretexting
entries.text: The lesson demonstrates pretexts through a LinkedIn HR message, a work-chat vendor request, and a WhatsApp coworker message. Those examples show that an invented identity or story can appear in more than one communication channel; verify the person and their authorization.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: You receive an email from your bank asking you to verify your account by clicking a link. What should you do? Contact the bank through a channel you already trust. Clicking the link or replying hands your details to whoever sent the email, and forwarding it spreads the risk to your colleagues.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: Which of these are common signs of a phishing email? (Select ALL that apply) Urgency, generic greetings and a mismatched sender domain are all common phishing signs, so all three should be ticked. An expected invite from a colleague's usual work account is normal activity.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: An email claims your account will be locked unless you act within 15 minutes. What is this technique called? A short deadline is meant to rush you past careful checking. Real security procedures, maintenance notices and system alerts do not threaten to lock you out within minutes unless you click.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: How does spear phishing differ from regular phishing? Spear phishing is aimed at a chosen person and uses details about them to look believable. It can arrive by email, text, chat or QR code, so it is not tied to one channel or device.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: A colleague sends you an urgent request to transfer funds to a new account. What should you do first? Call or message the colleague on a number or account you already have. Replying to the same message may reach the attacker, and a signature is easy to copy, so neither proves who sent it.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: You receive an email from your CEO asking for sensitive company data, addressed to you by name. What should you do? Attackers often pretend to be executives and use your real name. Replying goes back to the sender, and forwarding the data still sends it out, so check through a channel you already trust first.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: What is vishing? Vishing means voice phishing, done through phone or voice calls. Phishing by SMS is called smishing, and phishing with QR codes is called quishing.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: You receive a call from "tech support" claiming your computer is infected. They ask for remote access. What should you do? Real tech support does not make surprise calls asking for remote access. An employee ID is easy to make up, and asking them to call back keeps the scam going, so end the call and contact IT yourself.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: A caller claims to be from a government tax office and demands immediate payment by gift cards. What should you do? Government offices do not demand payment by gift card over the phone. A badge number can be invented, and negotiating still means paying the scammer, so hang up and call the office yourself.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: What is smishing? Smishing is phishing by SMS or text message. Email phishing is just called phishing, and phishing by voice call is called vishing.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: You receive a text message claiming you won a prize and need to click a link to claim it. What should you do? Surprise prize texts are a common smishing trick. Clicking or replying gives the scammer what they want, and forwarding it puts your friends at risk.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: You receive a text from your bank asking you to verify a transaction by clicking a link. What should you do? Check through the bank's own app or hotline. The link or a reply may go to a scammer, and ignoring it completely means a real problem with your account could go unnoticed.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: What is pretexting? Pretexting relies on a made-up story or role, like an auditor or new vendor, to make a request feel normal. Mass fake emails, software exploits and malware are different attacks.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: Someone claiming to be from IT asks for your password to "fix your account." What should you do? Real IT staff do not need your password. An employee ID can be faked, and any password you share, even a temporary one, can be used to get in.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: A delivery person asks for your full name and birth date to verify a package. What should you do? Couriers do not need your birth date to hand over a package. A company ID can be faked, and even part of your personal details can help someone steal your identity.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: What is quishing? Quishing means QR code phishing: the harmful link is hidden inside a QR code, so you cannot see where it goes before scanning. Quizzes, short links and fake invoices are other tricks.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: You see a QR code on a flyer promising a free gift. What should you do before scanning? Check where the code came from and look at the address your phone shows before opening it. Scanning first can already take you to a harmful page, and having a friend scan it only moves the risk to them.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: An email from "IT" asks you to scan a QR code with your phone to keep your work account active. What should you do? An unexpected QR code asking you to sign in should be treated like a suspicious link. Scanning it on any device opens the hidden page, and replying to the email only reaches the sender, who may be the attacker.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: Which password practice is most secure? A password manager lets you keep a long, unique password for every account. Reused or simple passwords are easy to guess or reuse after a leak, and shared passwords can no longer be controlled.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: What is two-factor authentication (2FA)? 2FA asks for two different kinds of proof, usually something you know and something you have. Two passwords are both things you know, and using two devices or two email accounts does not add a second check.

entries.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
entries.text: You receive an unexpected file attachment at work from a sender you do not know. What is the best thing to do? Leave it unopened and report it, so your IT or security team can check it and warn others. Antivirus does not catch every new threat, opening it risks infection, and replying confirms your address to the sender.
